Q: How to create and use a text file in Python? A:

You should use with open("textfile.txt", "w") as file, it's the best way.
But you can also use this:

file = open("textfile.txt","w")

file.write("something")

and make sure to do file.close() if you use the second method.

Q: EFI calling convention on RISC-V (illegal-instruction) A:

The code is supposed to follow a pointer chain, but your code doesn't do that. You are just increasing the pointer value without ever reading the memory. Here's how it should be (not tested but it should be closer to the truth):

.global _start
_start:
    addi sp, sp, -16        /* Adjust stack (should be 16-byte aligned) */
    /* no need to save t* and a* registers, they are caller-preserved */
    sd ra, 8(sp)  /* but do need to save ra so we know where to return to */
    sd fp, 0(sp)  /* and it is a good etiquette to establish proper frame structure */
    addi fp, sp, 16
    
    /* a1 points to SystemTable upon call to the entrypoint */
    ld a0, 64(a1)           /* Load SystemTable->EFI_SIMPLE_TEXT_OUTPUT_PROTOCOL into a0 */
    ld t2, 8(a0)            /* Load EFI_SIMPLE_TEXT_OUTPUT_PROTOCOL->OutputString into t2 */

    /* a0 keeps EFI_SIMPLE_TEXT_OUTPUT_PROTOCOL struct pointer as per OutputString proto */
    la a1, string_hello     /* a1 keeps CHAR16* string pointer */
    jalr ra, 0(t2)          /* Invoke EFI_SIMPLE_TEXT_OUTPUT_PROTOCOL->OutputString */
 /* jalr t2  <-- alternative shorthand notation for the same command as this is the most often used variation */

    ld ra, 8(sp)            /* Restore registers */
    ld fp, 0(sp)
    addi sp, sp, 16         /* Adjust stack */
    ret

Q: Error using Material 3 TextField: "None of the following candidates is applicable" A:

The immediate problem is that you call TextField with parameters that do not exist:

  • colors is expected to be of type TextFieldColors (which is a container for multiple colors), but you provide a Color (which is only a single color)
  • The parameter Value begins with a lower case v: value = ...
  • label takes a composable function as its value, not a String. Just wrap the value in curly braces: label = { Text(on_or_off) }
  • lineLimits only exists for the TextField overload that is based on a TextFieldState. When using a String value (like you do), though, you have to use the parameter singleLine = true instead.
  • placeholder takes a composable function as its value, not a String. Just wrap the value in curly braces: placeholder = { Text(stringResource(R.string.click)) }
  • The parameter Modifier begins with a lower case m: modifier = ...
  • You are missing the required parameter onValueChange which takes a lambda that is executed every time the user changes the content of the TextField.

That said, this won't work even with all of the above fixed. For starters, the TimePickerDialog doesn't work the way you use it. It is unclear why you even want to use the android.app.TimePickerDialog from the view system when you use Compose. Mixing these is usually not a good idea. There is a TimePicker composable that you could use instead (currently in alpha, so you would need to use the alpha Compose BOM), or you could simply write your own. Furthermore, timeToShow needs to be wrapped in a MutableState, otherwise Compose won't update the UI when that variable changes. And finally, it looks like you want to use the TextField to only display a value. If you don't want the user to interact with the text then you should consider using a simple Text composable, not a TextField.

I also glanced over the rest of your code from the GitHub repository you linked. There are a lot of rather severe errors in there (like the defunct Room setup, missing/wrong coroutine handling and the leaking Context). Some of it doesn't even look salvagable. You might want to go back to the drawing board and start from scratch.

Some pointers:

  • Use a layered architecture with view models.
  • Work through the Room code labs Persist data with Room and Read and update data with Room to learn how Room should be properly used with coroutines. Make sure all your DAO functions either return a Flow or are suspending - it must be exactly one of the two.
  • For the UI, only use Material 3 Compose components, no View components like the android.app.TimePickerDialog or ConstraintLayout and so on.
  • Don't use the obsolete and buggy java.util.Calendar class, use the classes from the java.time package if you insist on using Java. Better yet, though: Kotlin has native support for Clock and Instant, and the official kotlinx-datetime library provides LocalDate and LocalDateTime, among others.
  • Never pass Context to a composable. If you need a Context, use LocalContext.current.

Q: How do you avoid over-populating the PATH Environment Variable in Windows? A:

I wrote and use (on an every-time basis) a standard stream (stdin/stderr/stdout) & exit code PROXY program called Dispatcher.

All the CLI programs I use (node, php, python, git, svn, rsync, plink, ...) are actually the same exe file (around 10kb, that I just name differently); I put all the programs in the same directory.
A dummy static clear text file does the mapping from [proxy file name] to [real exe file].
Dispatcher uses low level Process management win32 API to be absolutely transparent.

Using this software, I only need ONE additional directory to be set in my PATH for all the programs I might want to use.
